massachusetts.damages_note: The fair monetary value of the decedent to the beneficiaries, including reasonably expected net income, services, protection, care, assistance, society, companionship, comfort, guidance, counsel, and advice, plus reasonable funeral and burial expenses. Punitive damages of at least $5,000 are available where the death was caused by malicious, willful, wanton, or reckless conduct or gross negligence. The recovery is divided among beneficiaries under ch. 229, § 1 (spouse and children first).
massachusetts.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death, or 3 years from the date the executor or administrator knew or should have known of the factual basis for the claim.
massachusetts.state_note: Massachusetts measures damages by the 'fair monetary value of the decedent' to the people who depended on them, and the recovery goes to the family beneficiaries rather than the estate itself. The claim is derivative: it can only be brought if the person who died could have sued for the injury had they lived.
massachusetts.who_can_file: Only the executor or administrator (personal representative) of the deceased person's estate may file the claim, for the benefit of the surviving spouse, children, and other beneficiaries listed in the statute (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 229, § 2).

michigan.damages_note: Reasonable medical, hospital, funeral, and burial expenses; the decedent's pain and suffering before death; loss of financial support and income; loss of society and companionship; and the survivors' mental anguish. There is no general cap on wrongful-death damages in Michigan, and punitive damages are generally not available.
michigan.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5805(2)). The deadline for the underlying claim can control instead (for example, 2 years for a medical-malpractice death), and a saving provision (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5852) may add time if the estate was opened within the original period.
michigan.state_note: The personal representative must notify all potential beneficiaries within 30 days of filing, and any settlement or distribution of the recovery needs probate court approval.
michigan.who_can_file: Only the personal representative of the deceased person's estate may file the claim, for the benefit of the surviving spouse, children, descendants, parents, grandparents, siblings, stepchildren, and anyone named in the will (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2922(2)-(3)).

minnesota.damages_note: Whatever the jury deems fair and just: the decedent's damages before death, the survivors' pecuniary loss, lost income and financial support, and loss of the decedent's services, protection, care, assistance, advice, comfort, companionship, and guidance. Funeral expenses are paid first out of any recovery. Punitive damages may be awarded under Minn. Stat. § 549.20.
minnesota.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death, and no more than 6 years after the wrongful act or omission. There is no deadline if the death was caused by an intentional act constituting murder. Deaths caused by medical malpractice follow the separate limits in Minn. Stat. § 541.076.
minnesota.state_note: Minnesota is unusual: family members cannot file directly. A court-appointed trustee brings the single claim for everyone, and the court decides how the recovery is divided among the survivors.
minnesota.who_can_file: The surviving spouse or next of kin petitions the court to appoint a trustee, and only that trustee may file the claim, for the exclusive benefit of the surviving spouse and next of kin (Minn. Stat. § 573.02, subds. 1, 3).

mississippi.damages_note: Whatever damages the jury determines to be just, considering all damages to the decedent and to every interested party, including lost income, medical and funeral expenses, loss of companionship, and the decedent's pain and suffering. Punitive damages may be available but are capped by state law. Non-economic damages are capped at $500,000 in medical-malpractice cases and $1,000,000 in product-liability cases.
mississippi.deadline_note: The deadline follows the underlying claim: generally 3 years from the date of death for a negligence death (Miss. Code Ann. § 15-1-49), but only 1 year if the death was caused by an intentional act such as assault or battery. Medical-malpractice deaths have shorter limits, and the clock runs from the wrongful act rather than starting fresh at death.
mississippi.state_note: Mississippi is one of the few states where close family members can file directly without opening an estate, and the statute also covers the death of an 'unborn quick child.'
mississippi.who_can_file: The personal representative of the estate, or the surviving spouse, children, parents, or siblings. Any one of them may file for the benefit of all, and there can be only one lawsuit for the same death (Miss. Code Ann. § 11-7-13).

missouri.damages_note: Whatever the jury deems fair and just: pecuniary loss, funeral expenses, and the reasonable value of the decedent's services, consortium, companionship, comfort, instruction, guidance, counsel, training, and support, plus the decedent's medical expenses and pain and suffering before death. The jury may also consider aggravating circumstances. There is no general cap, but non-economic damages in medical-malpractice deaths are capped under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 538.210.
missouri.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.100).
missouri.state_note: Missouri ranks who may sue in strict classes: a spouse, child, or parent outranks siblings, and siblings can only sue if no first-class family member is available. The claim belongs to the family, not the estate.
missouri.who_can_file: In strict priority order: first the surviving spouse, children (or descendants of deceased children), and parents; if there are none, the deceased's siblings or their descendants; if there are none, a court-appointed plaintiff ad litem. Only one action may be brought for the same death (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.080).

montana.damages_note: Economic losses (medical bills, funeral and burial expenses, lost wages and benefits) and non-economic losses (loss of companionship, love, support, and guidance, and grief and sorrow). Punitive damages are allowed only for actual fraud or actual malice and are capped at $10 million or 3% of the defendant's net worth, whichever is less (Mont. Code Ann. § 27-1-220).
montana.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death (Mont. Code Ann. § 27-2-204), or 10 years if the death resulted from homicide. Claims against a government entity have shorter notice requirements.
montana.state_note: Montana requires the wrongful-death claim and the survival claim (for the decedent's own losses) to be combined into one lawsuit, and each element of damages can be recovered only once (Mont. Code Ann. § 27-1-501).
montana.who_can_file: The personal representative of the deceased person's estate files the claim for the surviving family. If the person who died was a minor child, the parents (or legal guardian) may file (Mont. Code Ann. § 27-1-513).

nebraska.damages_note: Pecuniary (financial) losses only: reasonable funeral and burial expenses, medical bills, lost income and financial support, loss of companionship, care, and comfort, and the value of household services. Compensation for grief or mental anguish as such is not recoverable, and Nebraska's constitution bars punitive damages entirely. Medical-malpractice deaths are subject to a $2.25 million total cap (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 44-2825).
nebraska.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 30-810). The statute has no general discovery extension, so families should not count on extra time if the cause of death only becomes clear later.
nebraska.state_note: Nebraska's statute covers the death of an unborn child in utero, but no claim can be brought against the mother or against a provider who performed a consented medical procedure.
nebraska.who_can_file: Only the personal representative of the deceased person's estate may file the claim, for the exclusive benefit of the surviving spouse and next of kin (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 30-809, 30-810).

nevada.damages_note: Heirs may recover for grief or sorrow, loss of probable support, companionship, society, comfort and consortium, and the decedent's pain, suffering, or disfigurement. The estate may recover medical expenses, funeral expenses, and punitive damages the decedent could have recovered. There is no general cap on wrongful-death damages; medical-malpractice non-economic damages are capped under Nev. Rev. Stat. § 41A.035.
nevada.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (Nev. Rev. Stat. § 11.190(4)(e)). A claim against a government entity has a separate 2-year claim-filing requirement with the Attorney General.
nevada.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Center of Southern Nevada
nevada.state_note: Nevada is unusual in splitting the case in two: the heirs' claim and the estate's claim are separate and can be joined. The heirs' recovery is not liable for the decedent's debts, but the estate's recovery is. Anyone found liable for intentionally killing the person cannot bring or benefit from a claim.
nevada.who_can_file: The heirs of the person who died and the personal representative of the estate may each bring a claim. Heirs are the people who would inherit the person's separate property if there were no will (Nev. Rev. Stat. § 41.085).

new hampshire.damages_note: The decedent's mental and physical pain before death, reasonable medical, funeral and burial expenses, and lost earning capacity over the decedent's probable working life. A surviving spouse may also recover for loss of comfort, society, and companionship, capped at $500,000. Minor children (or parents of a minor child) may recover for loss of familial relationship, capped at $300,000 per claimant. Punitive damages are not available in wrongful-death cases.
new hampshire.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death (N.H. Rev. Stat. § 508:4). RSA 556:11 mentions a 6-year window, but it is expressly subject to RSA 508, so families should treat 3 years as the deadline.
new hampshire.state_note: New Hampshire has no standalone wrongful-death act: the dead person's own injury claim survives to the estate, with the death added as an element of damages. In 2025 the caps on loss-of-relationship damages were raised sharply (spouse from $150,000 to $500,000; minor child or parent from $50,000 to $300,000).
new hampshire.statute_name: New Hampshire Wrongful Death Statute (RSA chapter 556)
new hampshire.who_can_file: The administrator (or executor) of the deceased person's estate brings the claim. Under N.H. Rev. Stat. § 556:19, any person interested in the estate may start the action, but the administrator must take it over (N.H. Rev. Stat. §§ 556:12, 556:19).

new jersey.damages_note: Pecuniary (financial) losses only: loss of financial support, loss of services (including household services, guidance, and counsel), and reasonable medical, hospital, and funeral expenses. Grief, sorrow, and emotional anguish are not recoverable, and punitive damages are not available under the Wrongful Death Act.
new jersey.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (N.J. Stat. § 2A:31-3). There is no deadline for a claim against the perpetrator if the death was murder or manslaughter and the perpetrator was convicted, found not guilty by reason of insanity, or adjudicated delinquent. If a public entity may be at fault, a Tort Claims Notice is generally due within 90 days.
new jersey.state_note: New Jersey is one of the strictest states on damages: only money losses count, so the loss of companionship itself has no dollar value except as part of pecuniary loss. A separate Survival Act claim covers the decedent's own pain and suffering before death.
new jersey.who_can_file: Only the personal representative (executor or administrator) of the deceased person's estate may file, on behalf of the surviving spouse, children, parents, and others who would inherit under New Jersey's intestacy law (N.J. Stat. §§ 2A:31-1, 2A:31-2).
